items.title: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago
items.summary:
Bournemouth International Centre
Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements

Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer.

Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC were empty, a scenario completely congruous with his apparent indifference to the audience hellbent on deciphering his every syllable.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bob Dylan review – at 85, he is in finer voice now than he was 40 years ago

items.title: Novelist’s first album in eight years has Skepta, skits and soul – and showcases a true British original
items.summary:
(Mashwrks)
Sharp, unsentimental rhymes and a fearless disregard for genre make Scenes a richly varied victory lap for for one of grime’s most distinctive talents

It’s not often that a UK rap album arrives accompanied by its own air freshener and video game, but here we are. Head over to Novelist’s website, and you can find not merely the usual means of promoting a new release – branded hoodies, T-shirts and so on – but a scented mirror hanger that bears the album’s artwork and Scenes: the Drive, a vaguely Mario Kart-ish arcade game that involves driving around the landmarks of London and Los Angeles avoiding buses and the attentions of the traffic police to the strains of an album track called Prime.

But then, from the moment he appeared on the grime scene in his teens – so young he now constitutes an elder statesman in his late 20s – the south Londoner has cut something of a maverick figure in the world of UK rap. He arrived bearing a moniker that seemed oddly bookish among his more grittily named peers. His early releases saw him working alongside defiantly left-field producer Mumdance. He attracted a lot of press attention of the “grime’s brightest new hope” variety, but seemed to last about 20 minutes on the high-profile XL label before departing to start his own imprint, Mmmyeh.

Continue reading...

items.title: Amanda Seyfried was worried ‘You Can See Everything’ was going to “ruin her life”
items.summary:
Amanda Seyfried has said that getting involved in record-breaking documentary You Can See Everything was a “risk”.

READ MORE: ‘You Can See Everything’ review: a three-hour odyssey of deception, doubt and dodgy dealings 

You Can See Everything sees Nathan Fielder moving in with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her family in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment. After that initial batch of filming was complete, Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim reached out to Amanda Seyfried, who had previously played Holmes in dramatic biopic The Dropout , to get her take on the footage.

Seyfried went on to interview Holmes’ husband Billy Evans and stage recreations of conversations Fielder had with Holmes inside prison. “ I think I was the perfect replacement for the purpose of [Fielder] trying to understand her more ,” Seyfried explained during an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon earlier this week.

You Can See Everything has broken box office records in the US and the UK , and Seyfried could become the first documentary star to win an acting Oscar.

However in a new interview with Rolling Stone , she said getting involved in You Can See Everything felt like a huge risk. She agreed to take part without speaking to her lawyers, and had “no creative control” in what made it into the final cut.

“There was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything…

items.title: ‘I Am Legend’ director says the end was a failure despite box office success: “We didn’t approach it the way that we should have”
items.summary:
I Am Legend director Francis Lawrence has called the ending of the blockbuster a “failure” after it strayed away from what happened in the novel.

I Am Legend is based on Richard Matheson’s novel of the same name. The movie ends with Will Smith ’s Robert Neville fighting off a horde of infected humans while trying to find a cure for them, before he sacrifices himself to allow fellow survivors Anna (Alice Braga) and Ethan (Charlie Tahan) a chance to escape with the freshly-developed antidote. However in the book, it’s revealed that the Darkseekers are sentient and have started to create their own society, with Neville seen as a monster who butchers them in their sleep.

An alternative ending for I Am Legend was filmed that saw Neville realise that the Darkseekers weren’t mindless killers, so he refrained from blowing them up. In the years since the movie was released, fans have debated about which ending they preferred and now director Francis Lawrence has weighed in.

“I was obsessed with the last man on earth. We decided to set it in New York. Will (Smith), Akiva (Goldsman, producer) and myself basically came up with our version of the movie that we went out and made. My focus was on ‘what would it have been like for a person to have survived the collapse of civilisation,” he said during an appearance on the Team Deakins podcast. “What is it about the human spirit that prevents you from putting a gun in your mouth?”

View this post on Instagram 

“I wanted to make something more psychological and about social deprivation. Also, really get into the aspect of what would a…
items.t: ‘I Am Legend’ director says the end was a failure despite box office success: “We didn’t approach it the way that we should have”

items.title: ‘What A Talent’: Belinda Carlisle, UB40, Spandau Ballet & More Remember Andy Taylor
items.summary:
Tributes are flooding in for Andy Taylor , the brawny founding guitarist for Duran Duran and The Power Station, who has passed away after a years-long battle with prostate cancer. He was 65.

“I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor – such a genius… he played the guitar solo in MAD ABOUT YOU, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” writes Belinda Carlisle on her social channels .

“Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.”

Legendary Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant joined Taylor on stage in Oxfordshire, England back in 2023, at a charity fundraiser gig for The Cancer Awareness Trust. “A tough fighter, Andy Taylor,” he recounts , “like so many…some of us get through…condolences to his tribe,” he writes.

Fellow axeman Steve Stevens, the longtime talisman of Billy Idol, was heartbroken on the news. “F #ck cancer,” he writes . “Have so many memories with Andy. He was the first guitarist to sing my praises in the English press, I was forever grateful. He, Tony, & Robert are definitely jamming now,” says Stevens, a nod to the late Power Station members Tony Thompson and Robert Palmer.

Duran Duran and Spandau Ballet were, for a time, the British second invasion’s pin-up boys. “Spandau Ballet are deeply saddened by the passing of Andy Taylor,” reads a message from the pop group . “Andy was a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene that we were all proud to be part of.…

items.title: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?
items.summary:
Backed by the KLF, a monument is being built using 34,592 bricks, each containing a deceased person’s glazed ashes. Is this the future of funerals? We join emotional marchers on Birkenhead’s smoky, noisy Day of the Dead

Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people.

“My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA K2 Plant Hire Ltd), the seminal electronic duo and experimental art provocateurs, when they returned after 23 years in 2017.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘My brother was its first body’: would you add your corpse to Birkenhead’s pyramid of dead people?

items.title: Andy Taylor Was Full of Surprises: Six Deep-Dive Career Moments
items.summary:
Andy Taylor , the founding guitarist with Duran Duran , who passed away Monday (Nov. 23) following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, aged 65 , just might be the most underrated musician to emerge from the early 1980s.

Taylor, who would also form The Power Station, enjoyed a solo career and was something of a serial collaborator, stood tall in a golden era for electric guitarists. Even the slickest commercial pop songs had destructive guitar solos, the type of which seem to be lost to this generation and last.

Forget the Cold War, there was another arms race where the weapons of choice were plugged-in six-strings, with rows of effects pedals. Eddie Van Halen, Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, The Edge, Steve Stevens, Yngwie Malmsteen, Steve Lukather. It was an expansive group, and Andy Taylor was a member in good standing.

Born in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in north east England, Taylor was the wild boy in Duran Duran – his autobiography from 2008 even carried that title. 

Here was a roguish rockstar with fast hands, itchy feet, who didn’t follow trends, but had many, many followers. But because of his breakthrough with Duran Duran, a band that drew a mystifying flood of hate from critics of the time, Taylor’s talents were largely overlooked.

What he did next, couldn’t be ignored.

items.t: Andy Taylor Was Full of Surprises: Six Deep-Dive Career Moments

Cometh the hour, cometh U2 .

The legendary Irish rock band, as they’ve done so often in the past, stepped into the cauldron, rocked out, and gave everyone what they were looking for.

On this occasion, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. stepped into the colosseum that is the NFL’s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game at SoFi Stadium, pitting the Los Angeles Rams against the visiting Green Bay Packers.

The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix.

At the very top, the four bandmates took the long walk to the centerfield as a choir recited the lyrics of “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For.”

“Thank you for having us,” Bono remarked over Mullen’s iconic, military-style drum pattern that launched the mini-set proper with “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” one of the band’s early political anthems. The production stepped up several gears as a marching band assembled and the song shapeshifted, interpolating The Supremes’ “Stop! In The Name of Love.”

Then, a change in mood as U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton , the late queen of country’s smiling image splashed on three sails towering over the circular, center stage. Bono dueted with Dolly’s vocals for “Torn,” her very last recording which appears on the band’s 16th and latest studio album, Carnaval de Luz .

And, in a moment that earned a roar from the audience, the band slotted seamlessly into another Joshua Tree number, “Where The Streets Have No Name.” The sails came down, and U2 got down to rockstar business — with some support from scores of…

  • Andy Taylor – a life in pictures

It’s very easy indeed to paint Andy Taylor as the misfit within the world-beating five-man line-up of Duran Duran. The others were fans of glam and Chic: their avowed intention was to form a band that melded the sophisticated disco of the latter with the extravagant style and experimental art-pop of Roxy Music.

Taylor – who had made what he later called “that fateful journey down to Birmingham” from his home on Tyneside after spotting an ad in the Melody Maker – had tastes that tended towards rock music of a more traditional stripe, as evidenced by the artists he covered on his second solo album, 1990’s Dangerous: Thin Lizzy, Bad Company, AC/DC, Montrose.

items.t: Duran Duran was transformed by Andy Taylor’s rock edge – and never quite the same without him

items.title: Duran Duran’s Biggest Billboard Hits: ‘Rio,’ ‘Hungry Like the Wolf’ & More
items.summary:
Duran Duran charted 15 hits in the top 40 of the Billboard Hot 100 in 1983-93, a run of synth-pop classics, boosted by stylish videos amid MTV’s most tastemaking era, that led to the band ranking among the 100 top-performing acts in the chart’s history.

After John Taylor and Nick Rhodes formed the group in Birmingham, England, in 1978, Duran Duran — by then rounded out by lead singer Simon LeBon, Andy Taylor and Roger Taylor (with none of the Taylors related) — made its Hot 100 debut on Christmas Day 1982 with “Hungry Like the Wolf.” The following March, the single became the group’s first of 11 top 10s, reaching No. 3.

After “Rio” hit No. 14 in May 1983, two more Hot 100 top 10s followed that year: “Is There Something I Should Know” and “Union of the Snake.”

Duran Duran scored its first Hot 100 No. 1, “The Reflex,” in 1984 and added its second, “A View to a Kill,” in 1985, the latter marking the only leader on the list ever from the James Bond film franchise.

Later in the ‘80s, Duran Duran continued to scale the Hot 100’s top 10, while members posted hits via their own ventures, with Andy Taylor joining supergroup Power Station , which scored two top 10s in 1985: “Some Like It Hot” (No. 6) and “Get It On (Bang a Gong)” (No. 9).

Related

Plus, Andy Taylor — who, as announced Nov. 25, died at age 65 — reached No. 24 in 1986 with his solo song “Take It Easy.”

Meanwhile, Arcadia — LeBon, Rhodes and Roger Taylor — notched two top 40 Hot 100 hits in 1985-86, led by the No. 6-peaking “Election Day.”

The musician’s former bandmates shared the news Wednesday (Nov. 25) on their website and on Instagram , announcing that Taylor had passed away two days prior. “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the group wrote. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.”

Duran Duran continued, “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”

Still in its early years, the band added Taylor to the lineup in 1980. (Atlantic)
Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge

It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish.

Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits.

Relocating from Miami to Chicago for college, he frequented Gramaphone Records and Kstarke Records; spun at dives; and made beats as DJ Wey. items.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
items.summary:
He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse

For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US.

Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson

items.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe
items.summary:
Utilita Arena Cardiff
Kele Okereke has a tough challenge selling Bloc Party’s trite latest album – a far cry from Interpol’s ‘masterpiece’ eighth record, performed here to darkly hypnotic effect

Try as one might to resist comparison, the balance of this particular yin and yang has been shifting for some time. Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era.

Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners.

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
items.summary:
The Texas singer was fascinated by Elvis Costello as a kid and admires Nancy Sinatra’s sass and strength, but which of her own songs changed her life?

The first song I fell in love with
My mum gave me an old Dansette record player and a pile of albums. I must have been eight or 10, with my younger sister Corinne, getting butterflies to These Boots Are Made for Walkin’ by Nancy Sinatra. Years later, I read that she was told to sing it with a much more provocative attitude. You can hear the sass and the strength. Maybe that’s where my whole “don’t fuck with me” thing came from.

The song I do at karaoke
Give me any Marvin Gaye song, like You’re All I Need to Get By, and I’m all over it, but I’d normally pull someone up to duet with me.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I do a really good version of AC/DC’s Highway to Hell, which throws people’: Sharleen Spiteri’s honest playlist
